text: You get two binary trees, root and sub root. Return true if sub root shows up as a subtree of root. A subtree means one node of root plus all of its descendants.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the word all is doing a lot of work here. I need to find some node in root such that the whole tree hanging under it is identical to sub root. Same shape, same values, all the way down to the leaves. It is not enough that it starts the same way. Is that right?
That's right. All the way down.

Good. So there are really two different jobs in this problem. Job one is a search: pick a node in root to stand at. Job two is a check: at that node, compare two whole trees. They are not the same job, so I will write them as two functions.
Are there any constraints on the input size? And can values repeat, or can they be negative?
Root has between one and two thousand nodes, and sub root between one and a thousand. Values fit in the range minus ten to the fourth to ten to the fourth. Values can repeat.

Repeats matter. I can't stop at the first node whose value matches — several nodes may share that value and only one may be the real match. So the search has to keep going after a failed check. Let me run through the example: root is three, four, five, one, two and sub root is four, one, two. At node three the top values differ. At node four, the tree underneath is four with children one and two — exactly sub root. So the answer is true, and I never look at node five.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to collect every subtree of root into a list, then compare each one against sub root. That works, but building and storing all those trees is wasteful. I only need to visit each node once and test on the spot. This problem reminds me of a nested recursion: a tree-equality check, which walks two trees in lockstep, wrapped inside an ordinary traversal. It fits because the search is a traversal and the check is a two-pointer comparison. Two layers, two jobs.

Here's the plan. One: in the outer layer, an empty sub root is true and an empty root is false. Two: otherwise, try is-same right here, or search the left subtree, or the right subtree. Three: is-same returns p equals q when either side is null, else compares values and both child pairs. The outer layer joins with or and stops at the first place that works; the inner one joins with and and stops at the first difference. One thing worth flagging — that null line has to be p equals q, not return true when sub root runs out. Otherwise a tree that only starts like sub root, with extra nodes below, passes: root one, two, three, four against sub root one, two, three. The right answer is false. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The outer function guards the two empty cases, then tries is-same here, or recurses left, or right. The inner function is the plain same-tree check. One thing worth flagging — the single line return p equals q is carrying two cases at once. If both are null, it is true, which is how a leaf pair agrees. If exactly one is null, it is false, which is how the shapes are forced to match. One comparison, both jobs.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Root three, four, five, one, two, sub root four, one, two, expected true. The row that matters is is-subtree at node four: is-same agrees all the way down, so the or is satisfied and the right side, node five, is never evaluated. Two is-subtree calls, eight is-same calls. Let's also test with corner cases. The partial match, one, two, three, four against one, two, three: is-same hits four against null, so false. The official second example adds a zero under the two, and returns false. Single nodes: one against one is true, one against two is false. And a tree is always a subtree of itself.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of n times m: the outer walk visits the n nodes of root, and each can run a check costing up to m, sub root's size. The space complexity is O of the height of root, since a check never goes deeper than root itself. In the worst-case scenario, long chains of equal values, the bound is real. But in practice it is pessimistic: on random pairs, about sixty percent of is-same calls return at the very first value comparison. Oh, one more thing — the linear alternative is to serialize both trees with null markers and run a substring search, O of n plus m. It needs a delimiter before every value: otherwise the tree one, two serializes to one two followed by three hashes, which contains the string for a single node twelve — a false positive.

One assumption I should say out loud. My guard order checks an empty sub root before an empty root. That decides the both-empty case in favor of true — an empty sub root counts as present in any tree. The constraints say both trees have at least one node, so it never comes up on the judge. But it is a real choice, and if the caller could pass an empty sub root I'd want to agree on the answer first.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You split the problem into a search for a position and a check of a whole tree, then pointed out that the or and the and are the same short-circuit trick with opposite polarity. You named the partial-match trap before writing any code and brought a concrete counterexample for it. And when you offered the linear serialization alternative, you named the delimiter bug instead of hand-waving it. Good work.
